body:
Reasoning rules, part a of 2: evidence and measurement (M1-M15) and hypotheses H1-H7. TWENTY-TWO rules here, counted so a truncation is detectable; part b (reasoning-evidence-and-verification-b) holds H8-H15 and verification and test design T1-T14. Consolidated from migrated memories (Termal::Fable with Engram::Fable, 2026-09-07..11).

CARRYING A NUMBER
M1. Put subject, moment, unit, dimension and sample-or-bound in the same sentence as every number you report or relay. Why: a number that loses any of these keeps its precision and authority but loses its meaning ("5.1 s" of which store?).
M2. Attach the time of measurement; when a value and an action share a message, say which came first. Why: the work between measuring and sending makes the report stale; care does not shrink that window.
M3. When a reported value governs your next act, re-measure rather than quote. When two readings disagree, order them in time before deciding who erred. Why: both can be true of a subject that moved.
M4. Re-measure hardest the values you expect not to have changed. Why: an identical result confirms your belief and hides staleness; "unchanged" is the most dangerous outcome, not the neutral one.
M5. Treat internal consistency as evidence of a common source, never of currency. Why: a snapshot is consistent by construction, so a closed checksum of a superseded state is still closed. Consistency does detect mutilation, so announce item counts in any text a tool will later edit.
M6. Name cached copies and paths for what they are. origin/master is the last sync (git ls-remote asks the server). A path is not a content identity: name preserved copies by hash and check the hash before use. Why: the identifier survives while the thing it named moves.

READING AN INSTRUMENT
M7. Before attaching a claim to an instrument, write the instrument's question and the claim's question as two sentences and check that they match. Why: diff shape answers "same content?", not "arrived independently?"; path overlap counts filenames, not behavioural conflicts. Words about history (independently, separately, in parallel) need a record or a direct question to the party.
M8. Before reading a null result as a negative, ask whether the instrument could have seen the thing. Blind spots: scope (404 for "not yours"), time (a process table has no past), selection (a filter matching nothing exits 0, and cargo even says "ok"), audience (a printed signal nobody reads). File conflations that could be separated as defects; for constitutive ones, stop asking that instrument. Why: missing information makes people ask; wrong information makes them stop.
M9. A reading is not a property. Name the interval your decision covers and measure across it (the run, not the directory; the rate, not the level). For a growing quantity report a rate or a bound. Why: the dangerous claim is a truth that invites the wrong action.
M10. Count the driver before trusting a measurement of its effect. If the driver occurs zero times in the data, the structural bound from reading the code is the measurement. Why: precise numbers about an effect whose cause never happened are empty.
M11. Ask whether a mechanism is reachable from your caller, in your mode, and whether it arrives when it must, not whether it exists. Keep "registration accepted" and "invoked at the boundary" as separate records. Why: existence is almost always yes, and a hook that never fires raises no error.
M12. Settle availability with an attempt, not another read. Why: a schema proves a concept exists; only an attempt can fail informatively.

PRESERVING THE DISCRIMINATING FACT
M13. Record the discriminating fact while it still exists: the binary or tree a result came from, the negative control, fixture provenance, a contrary report. Do not edit code or tests during a gate: a measurement belongs to the binary that produced it. Why: afterwards every variant looks identical. A suspect number outranks a suspect test, because a false number lives for years in documentation.
M14. Before a mutation whose receipt you may not be able to read, record a baseline (fingerprint). If the outcome is unreadable, compare, instruct "do not retry", and state what remains unverified. Why: "unknown" is when people retry and double-apply; a hash proves that something differs, not how.
M15. Before recording an operator's observation as evidence for a change, verify the operator could be running it: served bundle time, and a grep for an identifier the change introduces. Attribute to the deployed set and name the changes that have no observation yet. Why: a happy user is not proof the last change made them happy.

FORMING AND TESTING HYPOTHESES
H1. State hypotheses in a form that can fail, and seek the observation that would refute them, not more that agree. Why: sightings consistent with both a hypothesis and its negation are no evidence, however many accumulate.
H2. Distrust a hypothesis that pleases you before it is checked. Check the boring explanation first and cheaply, give the interesting one to someone who can refute it, and write it as a question until checked. Why: the pleasure arrives before the evidence, and no such refutation that day was caught by its holder.
H3. Hand verification to someone who did not form the belief. Treat an agent refusing to shape evidence toward your hypothesis as the system working. Why: every correction came from outside.
H4. Look hardest where you feel certain, not where you worry. Why: doubt applies its own brake; certainty has none.
H5. Count agreeing reports from a channel that knew the hypothesis as one observation. The count means something only if some report could have gone against it and would still have been counted.
H6. Same-assumption agreement (the same helper or tool recomputing) says nothing about that tool. Only artefacts built on different assumptions can diverge, and divergence localises the error without guaranteeing which side is wrong.
H7. Test a generalisation on the adjacent case, not on the case it came from.

End of part a: 22 rules (M1-M15, H1-H7).
